title: Bernard's four loves
hookLine: Bernard of Clairvaux: we love ourselves, then God for our sake, then God for God's sake

lines: A MAP OF HOW LOVE GROWS.
cards: Someone drives to the airport at midnight to pick up a friend. The friend is grateful, and loves them a little more for it. That's not wrong; love often starts with what someone does for us.
But there's another kind too. A woman sits beside an old friend in a hospital, though he no longer knows her name. A father keeps loving a son who never calls.
Love that doesn't need a reason. A French monk once mapped how love grows from the first kind to the second. Today: Bernard's four loves.

teach.b: Bernard was the abbot of a monastery at Clairvaux in France, a Cistercian, part of a movement that wanted to live Benedict's Rule more simply and strictly. He preached, wrote, and advised popes.
One of his books is short: On Loving God. It opens by saying the reason for loving God is God, and the measure is to love without measure. Then he lays out four degrees of love.
The first: we love ourselves, for our own sake.

teach.h: SELF FOR SELF; GOD FOR SELF.
teach.b: Bernard doesn't scold this. It's where every human starts. A baby loves itself; it has to.
The second: we love God, but for our own sake. We turn to God because we need help, because life gets hard, because God gives us things. Again, Bernard isn't embarrassed by this.
The third: we love God for God's sake. Turning to God again and again, something changes, like a friendship that began with favors and became something else.
You start to love God not for what you get, but because God is good, and lovely in himself. And the fourth, which Bernard says is rare in this life: we love even ourselves only for God's sake.
We see ourselves the way God sees us, and love ourselves for that reason alone.
Elsewhere, preaching on the Song of Songs, Bernard puts love's highest form in a phrase people still repeat in Latin: amo quia amo, amo ut amem.
I love because I love; I love so that I may love. Love for love's sake. It needs no payment.

how: Christians, especially in Catholic and monastic traditions, read Bernard's On Loving God as a guide to prayer, and use his four degrees to examine what draws them to God.

o: the abbot who mapped four steps of love
a French poet who sang of courtly love
a mountain saint who rescued lost travelers

games.q: the four loves — tap the pairs.

s: Bernard scolds people for loving God for what they get
he calls it real, honest love, and a step on the way.
Bernard says the fourth love is rare in this life
loving even yourself only for God's sake.
amo quia amo means I love because I love
from his sermons on the Song of Songs.

games.q: you started turning to God because life got hard and you needed help. is that love, in Bernard's map?
o: yes: the second degree, real and honest.
only if you stop needing help.
games.why: Bernard calls it the second degree, and says turning to God again and again is how the third begins.

practice: Bring to mind someone you love and gently ask: what do I love them for? Let the honest answers come, what they give me, how they make me feel; that's the first step, and it's fine.
Then ask whether there's anything you love in them just because it's them, and stay with that. If you pray, you can ask the same about God.

wordCard.voice: Bernard, the abbot of Clairvaux who mapped four steps of love, ending in love that needs no reason. Self for self, God for self, God for God, and self for God.

orig.note: Latin: I love because I love; Bernard's phrase for love that needs no reason.

carryVoice: Your line: love for love's sake. I love because I love. That's day two hundred sixty-eight.
